newsitem.title: USA: Delta pilots seek wage increase, airline chief to retire.
newsitem.headline: Delta pilots seek wage increase, airline chief to retire.

text.p: Delta Air Lines Inc., in a surprise announcement, said Monday that Chief Executive Ronald Allen will retire and resign from the board of directors when his contract expires on July 31.

The abrupt decision ends Allen's 34-year career at the nation's third-largest airline and led to speculation about a rift with the board about Delta's strategic focus. Rumours also circulated on Wall Street that his departure would allow Delta to renew merger talks with Continental Airlines Inc.
The news coincided with an announcement by Delta's pilots that they will seek pay raises and work rule changes only a year after ratifying the current four-year contract with the airline.
The pilots' demands were driven by Delta's turnaround to record third-quarter profits and recent pay raises for non-union employees, spurred by union sacrifices under Allen's tenure.

"Recent events at both our company and in our industry raise serious questions about the fairness and equity of maintaining the status quo," they said. The pilots did not provide specific wage goals or work rule changes.

Delta's pilots' union said Allen's departure was "totally unexpected." The pilots' master executive council met with Allen on Monday, asking to reopen negotiations on a four-year contract its members ratified only one year ago.
Analysts said the pilots' efforts may be hampered as Delta seeks a new chief, who is likely wield a sharper cost-cutting knife and dampen bids for wage increases.

Allen, 55, who is also chairman and president of the carrier, will work with the board to find a successor and remain as a consultant and advisory director. He is credited with returning Delta to profitability following losses in the early 1990s.
"Certainly his departure seems abrubt. And perhaps not entirely voluntary, but that's just speculation," said Samuel Buttrick, an airline analyst with PaineWebber.
"One take could be that he wants to enjoy his life. It can be as simple as that," said Edward Starkman, an airline analyst with Dillon Read.

While some industry experts speculated Allen's departure would allow Delta's board to reopen merger talks with Continental, other experts said they doubted that this played a role in Allen's retirement.
The two carriers held merger discussions last fall. Allen had opposed the combination and those talks were quickly abandoned, analysts said.
Continental officials could not be reached for comment.

Delta also named Maurice Worth, executive vice president of customer service, as acting chief operating officer. Worth, 56, has 36 years of service at Delta in operations, station management and personnel.
Worth is one of three executive vice presidents at Delta who serve as members of the Executive Council with Allen. The Executive Council was formed in 1995 to set corporate policy and strategy.

Delta's pilots ratified a four-year contract in April 1996. Its provisions included a 2 percent pay cut in return for stock options, a profit-sharing plan comparable to those enjoyed by other Delta employees, a seat on the Atlanta-based company's board and improved retirement benefits.
At the time, Delta said it expected to save more than $750 million over the four years as a result of the collective bargaining agreement with the pilots.
Delta's pilots now contend that the situation has changed.
The union's master executive council said in a recorded message to the pilots that there is a "growing disparity between Delta's pilot compensation and the compensation of our peers in the industry."
Delta's stock rose 50 cents to $95 on the New York Stock Exchange.
